evidence.raw_text: Resolution Without Dissent: In-Path Per-Query Sanitization to Defeat Surreptitious Communication Over DNS

As one of the most fundamental Internet components, DNS has served various purposes and thus DNS traffic usually exhibits diverse patterns and is probably the least blocked by network administrators. These make DNS an attractive channel for attackers to establish surreptitious communications (i.e., DNS tunneling). In fact, such a surreptitious channel has been widely abused for command and control (C2) and enterprise-unapproved virtual private network (VPN). Existing approaches exclusively rely on the statistical characteristics of a sequence of DNS queries to detect DNS tunneling. Unfortunately, these approaches by nature cannot guarantee zero data leakage and can be evaded when the stolen data is exfiltrated over many root domains. As a result, stateof-the-art approaches are more suitable for threat investigation and forensic analysis, but not for DNS tunneling prevention. To fill this protection gap, we propose TunTight, the first system that is able to achieve in-path per-query DNS tunneling prevention. Our key insight is that DNS tunneling domains have unique characteristics in their authoritative nameservers, domain usage, and domain name patterns. Based on these characteristics, a set of unique features are defined and extracted which are fed to a machine learning model. To validate the efficacy of TunTight, we integrate it into the cloud backend of an enterprise firewall product by one of the largest security vendors. In our two-months real-world deployment, TunTight has successfully detected 349 confirmed tunnels at the very first query with negligible false positives and negatives. We also conduct the first large-scale study of DNS tunneling activities in the wild. One interesting finding is that most DNS tunneling traffic in enterprise networks come from public tunneling tools and enterprise-unapproved VPN services. 1. Existing approaches exclusively rely on the statistical characteristics of a sequence of DNS queries to detect DNS tunneling. Unfortunately, these approaches by nature cannot guarantee zero data leakage and can be evaded when the stolen data is exfiltrated over many root domains. As a result, state- of-the-art approaches are more suitable for threat investigation and forensic analysis, but not for DNS tunneling prevention. To fill this protection gap, we propose TunTight, the first system that is able to achieve in-path per-query DNS tunneling prevention. Our key insight is that DNS tunneling domains have unique characteristics in their authoritative nameservers, domain usage, and domain name patterns. Based on these characteristics, a set of unique features are defined and ex- tracted which are fed to a machine learning model. To validate the efficacy of TunTight, we integrate it into the cloud backend of an enterprise firewall product by one of the largest security vendors. In our two-months real-world deployment, TunTight has successfully detected 349 confirmed tunnels at the very first query with negligible false positives and negatives. One interesting finding is that most DNS tunneling traffic in enterprise networks come from public tunneling tools and enterprise-unapproved VPN services. 1. Introduction Surreptitious communication over DNS (also known as DNS tunneling ) has become one of the most severe security threats that enterprises have to tackle. When cybercriminals sneak into an enterprise's internal network and gain access to sensitive data, they can exfiltrate the stolen data out of the enterprise over DNS traffic [ 1][ 2]. Another common use case of DNS tunneling is to set up a bi-directional communication channel through which attackers can es- tablish command and control (C2) with the compromised internal hosts and conduct further reconnaissance. Such a bi-directional communication channel can also be abused as a VPN to bypass network security and control policies of an enterprise, e.g., obtaining free Internet services [ 3]. This kind of abused VPN is referred to as enterprise-unapproved. Compared to other surreptitious communication chan- nels, DNS has several unique characteristics and properties attractive to attackers. As a fundamental component of the Internet, DNS is used by the vast majority of network ap- plications. Therefore, modern enterprise networks, including the most security-conscious ones, often have to allow hosts to send and receive DNS traffic. Even worse, some enter- prise networks fail to implement proper control policies, allowing arbitrary egress and ingress DNS traffic. Moreover, a client on average can send around 20K DNS queries per day [ 68] and an enterprise network can contain thousands of clients. Such a huge amount of DNS traffic serves as a great cover for DNS tunneling activities. Many efforts have been devoted to DNS tunneling de- tection in the past [ 51][ 52][ 58][ 67][ 46]. All of these approaches are based on the fact that one DNS message can only convey a limited amount of data and thus it is inevitable for attackers to send out many DNS queries within a short time window. As such, the statistical characteristics of a se- quence of DNS queries for the fully qualified domain names (FQDNs) under the same root domain 1 can provide highly promising detection capability. Unfortunately, these volume- based statistical approaches suffer two shortcomings. First, they by nature cannot prevent data being leaked in the first few queries. In practice, even partially leaked sensitive data ( e.g., a few passwords) could pose a perennial threat and incur irreparable losses to enterprises. Second, attackers can exfiltrate data using many different root domains, with one single query to each in the extreme case. Such a sophisticated evasion strategy has been adopted in advanced persistent threats (APT) [ 4]. Due to these shortcomings, existing approaches are more suitable for threat investigation and forensic analysis, but not for real-time detection and prevention. In this paper, we develop TunTight, a machine learn- ing based detector with the primary goal to detect and block 1. To achieve this, TunTight leverages the character- istics derived solely from every single query. We formulate the DNS tunneling characteristics from three aspects. First, we notice that attackers commonly set up their own author- itative nameservers (aDNS) so that the tunneling channel is reliable and supports bi-directional communications. These aDNS servers are usually dedicated and have low reputation. By contrast, the vast majority of non-tunneling domains prefer managed aDNS services such as those provided by domain registrars and cloud platforms. Accordingly, four unique features are defined for our machine learning model. Second, legitimate domains with tunneling-like traffic can often be attributed to specific Internet services owned by known organizations. Tunneling domains owned by attack- ers instead generally have no indicator of benignity. Based on this observation, we extract two additional unique fea- tures. Finally, DNS tunneling in practice dominantly en- codes data in the query name field of a DNS message. This leads to distinguishing differences in the queried domain names between tunneling and non-tunneling traffic. For instance, tunneling domains often comprise a long sequence of random characters, compared to a short sequence of meaningful words in non-tunneling domains. To characterize this pattern, we compute three features, with one being first proposed in TunTight. These nine features are then used to train an unsupervised machine learning model, specifi- cally Isolation Forest (IF) [ 62]. To validate the efficacy of TunTight, we perform comprehensive and in-depth evaluations. During our of- fline analysis using labeled datasets, we demonstrate that with an appropriate detection threshold for our IF model, TunTight can accurately detect all tunneling queries that are generated by both APT malware and VPN services. In addition, TunTight incurs negligible latency and thus it is efficient enough to be deployed on recursive resolvers for in- path protection. To the best of our knowledge, TunTight is the first system that is able to achieve in-path per-query DNS tunneling prevention. We further integrate TunTight into the cloud backend of an enterprise firewall product, Advanced DNS Security by Palo Alto Networks [ 44]. In our two-months real-world deployment, TunTight inspects 253 billion queries from about 30K organizations across the globe. The results are quite promising, with 358 tunneling root domains being detected and confirmed. More importantly, all of these tun- neling activities are detected within six queries, with 349 being detected at the very first one. Our manual analysis finds that most of these tunneling traffic comes from public tunneling tools and enterprise-unapproved VPN. There are 63 false positives (FPs) and 20 false negatives (FNs). All 63 FPs are low-profile domains and most of them could be eliminated with improved algorithms of feature computa- tion. The 20 FNs are actually a subset of the 358 detected domains. This indicates that TunTight might miss some tunneling queries, but eventually all tunneling activities can be detected. Surreptitious Communication over DNS Since most enterprise networks implement relatively permissive policies for DNS traffic, surreptitious commu- nication over DNS has become a usual modus operandi by adversaries to bypass enterprises' network security and control policies. Specifically, adversaries can tunnel mali- cious communications ( e.g., C2 and data stealing) through normal DNS queries and responses. Therefore, surreptitious communication over DNS is also commonly referred to as DNS tunneling. As shown in Figure 1, the bi-directional communication over DNS tunneling is called DNS exfiltration and infiltra- tion, respectively. In both cases, there is a compromised host, either hacked by external attackers or abused by insiders, within the victim enterprise network. The compromised host usually conducts domain resolution via an internal DNS resolver owned by the enterprise. Furthermore, a firewall is commonly deployed on the edge of an enterprise network for security enforcement and traffic control. In order to bypass firewalls and exfiltrate the data stolen from an enterprise network, an adversary first registers a root domain ( e.g., exfil.example in Figure 1) and sets up the aDNS for it or its subdomains. Then, the stolen data is encoded in DNS queries which are subsequently sent to the internal resolver, the same as other normal DNS queries. The in- ternal resolver conducts iterative resolution and eventually forwards the data-encoded queries to the attacker-controlled aDNS.
